newsitem.title: UK: Talks fail to ease N.Irish parades tension.
newsitem.headline: Talks fail to ease N.Irish parades tension.

text.p: British-sponsored talks aimed at reducing tensions during Northern Ireland's volatile "marching season" ended after eight hours on Friday without agreement, participants said.

"While we have not reached a resolution today, there are a number of areas which I want to consider further, " Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mowlam said in a statement. "I shall do this and be in touch again with both sides early next week."

Mowlam brought Roman Catholic objectors and Protestant parade organisers under the same roof, although they stayed in separate rooms, to try to reach a compromise about the most hotly-disputed pro-British procession, due to be held in Portadown on July 6.
The Catholics, from an Irish nationalist enclave on the march route, blamed the Protestant Orange Order for the impasse, saying it had refused to talk to them face-to-face.

"We had useful and constructive exchanges during the course of the day with the secretary of state (Mowlam)," the Catholic group said in a statement. "Unfortunately the Orange Order were not willing to pursue a similar path with us directly."

But the Orangement, who say their Portadown parade is a simple demonstration of religious faith, issued a statement saying they had put forward "respnsible and accommodating principles which respect the rights of everyone."
Both sides said they wanted a peaceful resolution to the controversy over the parade in Portadown, a town where sectarian tensions run high.
British sources said Mowlam might hold separate meetings with the two sides at Drumcree next week but they stressed that time was running out for an agreement.

Britain fears that any trouble at the Portdown parade could ignite violence across the province. The security climate worsened last week when the Irish Republican Army, fighting to end rule from Britain, shot dead two police officers in the town of Lurgan.
New Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern, who succeeded John Bruton on Thursday, spoke by telephone to British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Friday and will meet him next Thursday, officials said.

Blair, in a statement to parliament on Wednesday, outlined an Anglo-Irish strategy for taking guerrilla weaponry out of the Northern Ireland arena in hopes of reaching a political settlement in the province by next May.

He said that, three days before the Lurgan shootings, Britain told Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, that it could enter peace talks six weeks after guerrillas committed themselves to an unequivocal end to violence.
